screens.title: The Rise of Ethereum: Beyond Digital Currency
screens.narratorSegment: In this short course we will follow a single idea: Ethereum took blockchain beyond money. You will learn how smart contracts let code run as enforceable agreements, how the Ethereum Virtual Machine gives every node the same execution environment, what differentiates externally owned accounts from contract accounts, and why gas is central to safe, predictable execution. We will use concrete examples, like a freelance payout automated by a contract and examining real transactions on a block explorer to ground each concept. Understanding this foundation matters because it changes how you design software: no central server enforces outcomes, the network does. A common misconception is to treat Ether as only a currency — instead think of it as fuel that permits computation. By the end of these slides you will be able to explain why Ethereum’s design choices enable decentralized applications, identify when Ethereum is a better fit than a simple-value ledger, and read a transaction fee calculation. As you start, notice the three topics listed below: comparison to Bitcoin, the smart contract model, and practical mechanics like EVM and gas. Which of those seems most important to your project right now?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next slides you will build a clear mental model of how Ethereum differs from earlier blockchains and the mechanics that make it programmable. First, you will learn to distinguish Ethereum from Bitcoin by comparing their goals and scripting capabilities, which matters when choosing a platform. Second, you will form a working definition of a smart contract: a self-executing program stored on the blockchain, and you will see concrete examples such as automated payouts or scheduled distributions. Third, you will understand the EVM as the deterministic runtime that every node executes, and why determinism and a stack-based architecture are essential for consensus. Fourth, you will learn to identify the two account types—externally owned accounts controlled by private keys and contract accounts controlled by code—and why that distinction affects security and interactions. Each objective includes a small milestone to verify understanding so you can practice reading a transaction, spotting a contract address, or explaining a fee calculation. By the end of these objectives you will know not just what each component is, but why it matters in design choices and cost trade-offs when building dApps.

screens.title: Bitcoin vs Ethereum: design philosophies
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the difference in purpose. Bitcoin's core innovation was a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that focuses on secure value transfer and intentionally limited scripting to reduce risk and complexity. Ethereum was designed from the outset to be a platform for arbitrary computation and programmable agreements — a world computer that can run smart contracts. That difference is not academic: a limited scripting language reduces the attack surface and keeps the protocol simple, while a Turing-complete environment increases flexibility but also opens new categories of risk and cost. A concrete example: Bitcoin scripts can validate simple spending conditions like multi-signature or time-locks. Ethereum smart contracts can implement a full escrow workflow that holds funds, checks off conditions, and releases payment automatically. A common misconception is that one is strictly "better" than the other; instead they are designed for different trade-offs. When deciding which chain to use, ask whether you need arbitrary business logic on-chain. If so, Ethereum’s model and the EVM are purpose-built for that work. As a takeaway, think about your application requirements: if you need programmability and on-chain enforcement, Ethereum is the better fit; if you only need a secure, minimal settlement layer, Bitcoin’s constraints may be desirable.

keyIdea.title: Why the difference matters
keyIdea.text: Bitcoin optimizes for secure value transfer with limited scripting; Ethereum optimizes for on-chain programmability with smart contracts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Bitcoin vs Ethereum
Core Concept
Philosophy & Trade-offs
Compare goals, security, and scripting power with practical examples and a common decision rule.
Bitcoin: Secure value transfer, limited scripting, simpler risk profile.
Ethereum: Programmable logic, arbitrary computation, higher surface for complex apps.
Decision rule: Choose Ethereum if your app needs on-chain enforcement of business logic.
Key Takeaway

Different design goals lead to different tooling: Bitcoin for settlement, Ethereum for programmable applications.

Concrete example — Automated escrow
An escrow smart contract holds funds and releases them when predefined conditions are met, with no third party needed.
Steps in escrow contract
  • Client deposits funds into contract.
  • Freelancer submits work and a verification flag is set.
  • Contract logic verifies and releases funds automatically.
Common misconception
Programmability means "free" features — in fact every on-chain operation requires gas and design trade-offs matter.
Check your understanding
If you needed immutable message storage only, would Ethereum or Bitcoin be a better fit? Why?

screens.title: What is a Smart Contract?
screens.narratorSegment: A smart contract is a program stored on the blockchain that runs exactly as programmed when triggered by transactions. Think of it as a self-executing agreement: the terms are written in code and enforced by the network instead of a court or a central server. A concrete example is a freelancer payment contract that releases funds once the job status is set to complete. Because the code and state are stored on-chain, results are immutable and censorship-resistant. That immutability is powerful but comes with caveats: bugs cannot be patched without careful upgrade patterns, and every operation costs gas to execute. One common misconception is to equate a smart contract with a legal contract; they are not the same. Smart contracts enforce coded logic, but they may not address off-chain disputes or real-world verification unless the contract is paired with oracles or other verification mechanisms. In practice, designers must decide which parts of a workflow belong on-chain and which remain off-chain to balance transparency, cost, and upgradability. As a takeaway, define a small on-chain core of trustless logic and keep heavy or mutable processes off-chain. How would you split responsibility for a payments workflow between on-chain code and an off-chain verifier?

keyIdea.title: Smart Contract essence
keyIdea.text: A smart contract is on-chain code that executes deterministically and autonomously, enforcing the coded rules without intermediaries.

content.html:
Core Concept › Smart Contract
Smart Contract — definition and implications
Self-executing program stored on-chain that enforces terms without a third party.
Immutable once deployed unless upgrade patterns are used.
Every on-chain operation consumes gas and costs Ether.
Can interact with EOAs and other contracts through messages and calls.
Requires careful testing and audits because code becomes policy.
Concrete example: Freelancer payout
Client deposits funds to the contract. When verification is set true, the contract releases the funds to the freelancer automatically, removing reliance on a trusted escrow agent.
Why this matters
Smart contracts enable dApps, decentralize control, and let value flow without intermediaries.
Key Takeaway

Use smart contracts for on-chain enforcement, but plan upgrades and off-chain checks for real-world data.

Misconception
A smart contract is not a legal contract by itself; it is a technical mechanism that enforces coded rules.

screens.title: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
screens.narratorSegment: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the runtime environment that executes smart contract bytecode on every participating node. Conceptually, you can think of the EVM as a global, decentralized computer: when a transaction calls a contract function, the contract’s bytecode is executed by the EVM to produce a new state. Because the same bytecode runs on every node, determinism is essential — all nodes must agree on the result to reach consensus. The EVM is stack-based: operations push and pop values to a stack, which is simpler to reason about for bytecode interpretation. It is also Turing-complete, meaning it can represent any computation given enough resources. However, the EVM limits resource consumption through gas so that long-running or infinite computations are impossible without payment. A concrete example is a token transfer function: its bytecode updates balances and emits an event; every node runs those same steps and updates local state identically. A common misconception is to imagine the EVM as a single machine; in reality, it is a replicated execution environment running independently on many machines to ensure the same result. As a takeaway, design contracts to be deterministic and gas-aware so the EVM can run them efficiently and securely.

keyIdea.title: EVM essence
keyIdea.text: The EVM is a replicated, deterministic runtime that executes smart contract bytecode and enforces consensus across nodes.

content.html:
Process Flow › Ethereum Virtual Machine
How the EVM executes contract code
Deterministic, stack-based, and replicated across nodes to maintain consensus.
Step 1 — Transaction is submitted
An externally owned account signs and sends a transaction calling a contract function or deploying code.
Step 2 — Nodes run the EVM
Every participating node executes the contract bytecode within its EVM instance, following the same instructions to update state.
Step 3 — Deterministic state changes
Because execution is deterministic, nodes reach the same new state and the network advances securely.
Key Takeaway

The EVM ensures consistent results across many machines; gas limits prevent runaway computation.

Stack-based execution: operations push and pop values.
Turing-complete: expressive but resource-limited by gas.
Concrete example: token transfer
A transfer function updates sender and recipient balances and emits an event. Every node applies the same bytecode changes.
Misconception
The EVM is not a single central computer but many replicated runtimes that must agree on results.

screens.title: Ethereum Accounts: EOAs and Contract Accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Ethereum distinguishes two account types that are central to how users and contracts interact. Externally Owned Accounts, or EOAs, are controlled by private keys held by people or services; they can sign transactions, send Ether, and call contracts. Contract Accounts are controlled by code: they are created when a contract is deployed and have no private key. They can hold Ether and tokens, and they execute their code when called by an EOA or another contract. A concrete example: using a wallet like MetaMask manages an EOA — you sign a transaction that calls a contract method to swap tokens. The contract account then runs its code and updates storage and balances. A common misconception is to assume that contract accounts 'belong' to a person — in reality they act by their code and any privileges are encoded into that code. Security implications flow from this distinction: EOAs custody private keys and are susceptible to private key compromise, while contract accounts are susceptible to logic bugs. As a takeaway, when designing a dApp, explicitly decide which operations require human signatures and which should be delegated to contract logic, and plan key management and upgradeability strategies accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Account distinction
keyIdea.text: EOAs are key-controlled user accounts; contract accounts are code-controlled identities that execute when invoked.

content.html:
Definition › Ethereum Accounts
Account hierarchy and control
Two account types with different controllers and permissions.
EOA: controlled by a private key; can sign transactions and pay gas.
Contract Account: controlled by code; no private key; executes when called.
Interactions: EOAs call contracts, contracts call other contracts, and both can hold Ether.
Concrete scenario
You sign a transaction with your wallet (EOA) to call a DeFi contract (contract account) to swap tokens. Your EOA pays gas and the contract executes the swap logic.
Security note
Protect private keys for EOAs and audit contract code for contract accounts. Each has a different threat model.
Common Mistake

Assuming a contract account is a 'wallet' you can control like an EOA. Contract behavior depends solely on code logic.

Key Takeaway

Design clear boundaries: which actions require human signing and which run autonomously in contract logic.

screens.title: Gas: the unit of computational effort
screens.narratorSegment: Gas is a measure of computational effort on Ethereum. Every basic operation in a transaction or contract execution consumes a specific amount of gas. When you submit a transaction you specify a gas limit and a gas price; validators execute instructions and charge for the gas used. The essential purpose of gas is twofold: it prevents malicious or accidental infinite loops and runaway computation by making each operation cost something, and it fairly compensates validators for processing transactions. A concrete analogy in the chapter is fuel for a car: Ether is the currency used to pay for gas, which is the resource measured during computation. A common beginner mistake is to think of gas as a separate currency — it is actually a unit, and you pay for it in Ether; the fee equals gas used times gas price. Another practical point is that gas prices change with network demand, so complex operations are more expensive during congestion. As a takeaway, always estimate gas for your smart contract functions and design gas-efficient logic so users do not face unexpectedly high costs.

keyIdea.title: Gas purpose
keyIdea.text: Gas quantifies computational work to prevent abuse and to reward validators, paid in Ether according to Gas Used times Gas Price.

content.html:
Definition › Gas
What gas is and why it matters
A unit that measures the cost of computation; paid in Ether to validators.
Purpose
Prevents infinite loops and resource spam, and rewards validators for work.
Analogy
Think of gas as mileage: operations consume units and you pay for those units with Ether as fuel.
Practical tip
Estimate gas for contract functions and avoid expensive patterns during heavy usage periods.
Key Takeaway

Gas enforces economic limits on computation and aligns incentives for validators through fees.

Common misconception
Gas is not a separate coin — it is a unit you pay for with Ether; fees equal Gas Used times Gas Price.
Why gas price matters
If you set a low gas price, validators prioritize other transactions and your transaction may be delayed or never included.

screens.title: Transaction Fees: Gas Used × Gas Price
screens.narratorSegment: A practical formula you will use repeatedly is simple: total transaction fee equals Gas Used times Gas Price. Gas Used is the actual number of gas units consumed while executing your transaction or contract call. Gas Price is how much Ether you are willing to pay per gas unit. Combined they yield the fee paid in Ether. For example, if a transaction uses 50,000 gas and the gas price is 20 gwei, multiply those to get the transaction cost (in this case convert gwei to Ether to get the final amount). Why does this matter? Because both factors affect cost and latency: higher gas price encourages validators to include your transaction sooner, and more complex contract operations increase gas used. A common misconception is to ignore Gas Used when estimating cost — optimizations that reduce gas used directly reduce user expense. Another important detail from the chapter is that network demand makes gas prices vary, so the same operation can cost more or less depending on congestion. As a takeaway, always test and estimate gas consumption for common functions and communicate likely costs to users so they can make informed decisions about interacting with your dApp.

keyIdea.title: Fee calculation
keyIdea.text: Transaction fee = Gas Used × Gas Price. Lower gas use and competitive gas price reduce cost and speed processing.

content.html:
Process › Fee Calculation
Calculate transaction fees
Use the formula and understand variables that change cost and speed.
// Formula
// Fee = Gas Used × Gas Price
// Example values shown conceptually
Gas Used = 50000
Gas Price = 20 gwei
Fee (in gwei) = 50000 * 20 = 1,000,000 gwei
// Convert gwei to ether as needed for final fee
Practical example
If a transfer uses 21,000 gas and gas price spikes, the same transfer costs more during congestion. Estimating gas prevents surprises.
Common mistake
Ignoring variable gas price when planning operations — always consider peak and off-peak costs.
Key Takeaway

Both gas used and gas price determine cost; optimize gas use and set appropriate gas price for timeliness.

Why validators care
Validators prioritize transactions by gas price because it determines their reward; higher price increases priority.
User-facing tip
Show estimated fee ranges in your dApp and recommend gas price choices based on current demand.

screens.title: Bytecode, Deployment, and Execution
screens.narratorSegment: When you deploy a smart contract, the compiler produces bytecode that is stored on-chain as the contract account’s code. That bytecode is what the EVM executes when the contract is called. Deployment is itself a transaction: it stores the bytecode in a new contract account and consumes gas proportional to code size and constructor work. When a user later calls a function, the transaction provides input data and the EVM steps through the bytecode deterministically, updating storage and producing any events or returns. A concrete example: a simple token contract compiles to bytecode that implements balance updates, transfer checks, and emits events. A common misconception is to think source code is required at runtime — the EVM only runs bytecode; source code may be verified and published for human readability, but the network executes compiled code. As a developer, remember that deployment costs can be large because storing code on-chain consumes gas; that is why minimizing unnecessary code and using libraries or proxy patterns can be important. Consider deployment as an investment: once code is stored immutably, its behavior governs future interactions unless upgrade patterns are used.

keyIdea.title: Deployment fact
keyIdea.text: Contracts are deployed as bytecode; the EVM executes that bytecode and deployment itself consumes gas.

content.html:
Code › Bytecode & Deployment
From source to bytecode to execution
Deployment stores bytecode; calls execute that code on the EVM.
// Conceptual flow
// 1. Write smart contract source
// 2. Compile -> bytecode
// 3. Deploy transaction stores bytecode in a contract account
// 4. Calls run bytecode on the EVM, consuming gas
// Note: EVM executes bytecode deterministically on every node
Deployment cost note
Storing code increases gas used during deployment. Minimize unnecessary code and use lightweight initialization where possible.
Key Takeaway

Bytecode is the runtime artifact; plan for deployment costs and immutability when releasing contracts.

Misconception
Source code publication is for humans. The network executes compiled bytecode only.
Concrete example
A token deploy stores balance mapping logic; calls to transfer update those mappings deterministically through bytecode execution.

screens.title: Exploring the Blockchain with a Block Explorer
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most useful hands-on skills is reading live data on the blockchain through a block explorer. Start by finding the latest block and observe fields like block height, timestamp, number of transactions, gas used, and the parent hash which links to the previous block. Then click a transaction to see details such as transaction hash, status, from and to addresses, value, gas used and gas price. When you inspect an address, check whether it is an externally owned account or a contract account; verified contracts often show source code and separate read and write sections. A concrete exercise is to search for a known contract address and open the 'Contract' tab to explore read functions like name() or symbol() for a token. This practice demonstrates blockchain transparency: anyone can audit code and transactions. A common beginner pitfall is not interpreting gas fields correctly; gas used is the actual consumption, while gas limit is the cap set by the sender. As a takeaway, regular use of a block explorer will strengthen your intuition about on-chain state changes and help you validate behavior before and after deploying contracts.

keyIdea.title: Explorer practice
keyIdea.text: Use a block explorer to inspect blocks, transactions, and verified contract functions to reinforce understanding of on-chain data.

content.html:
Process › Block Explorer Walkthrough
Inspect blocks, transactions, and contracts
A step-by-step exercise to build intuition from live data.
Step 1 — Latest blocks
Observe block height, timestamp, transactions, gas used, and parent hash to follow chain progression.
Step 2 — Transaction details
Open a transaction to view status, hash, from/to, value, gas used, and gas price.
Step 3 — Inspect a contract
If verified, read public functions and try reading values via 'Read Contract' to see transparency in action.
Common Pitfall

Confusing gas limit with gas used. Gas limit is a cap you set; gas used is what the transaction actually consumed.

Key Takeaway

Regularly inspect transactions and contracts to validate expected behaviour and to estimate real costs.

screens.title: dApps: Decentralized Applications and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Decentralized applications, or dApps, combine a smart-contract backend with often an open-source frontend to deliver user experiences that do not rely on a centralized server. The chapter lists several domains where dApps are prevalent: financial services in DeFi, gaming and digital collectibles like NFTs, and supply chain solutions. The enabling property is that the backend logic is on-chain and enforceable by the network. A concrete example is a lending protocol where smart contracts govern collateral, interest rates, and liquidation rules — all executed without a single counterparty. This removes the need to trust a central operator but requires careful design around upgradability and governance. A common misconception is that dApps are automatically private; on the contrary, most on-chain activity is transparent and publicly auditable. When choosing patterns for a dApp, weigh decentralization benefits against transparency and cost. As a takeaway, dApps are powerful where trust minimization and verifiable enforcement create value, but they demand attention to gas costs, security, and whether parts of the workflow should remain off-chain for privacy or efficiency. dApps: Decentralized Applications and Use Cases means dapps use smart contracts for backend logic to enable trust-minimized, verifiable applications across finance, collectibles, and beyond.. In practical terms, from defi to nfts — how smart contracts enable new application classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: dApp essentials
keyIdea.text: dApps use smart contracts for backend logic to enable trust-minimized, verifiable applications across finance, collectibles, and beyond.

content.html:
Comparison › Decentralized Applications
What makes a dApp
An on-chain smart contract backend paired with a user-facing frontend to create a decentralized service.
DeFi: lending, exchanges, and automated market makers.
NFTs: tokenized collectibles with on-chain provenance.
Gaming: on-chain assets and marketplaces.
Supply chain: verifiable tracking and immutable logs.
Key Takeaway

dApps deliver trust-minimized services but require careful design around cost, privacy, and upgradeability.

Concrete example
A lending dApp encodes collateral rules on-chain so loans are issued and liquidated based on contract logic, not a central party.
Misconception
dApps are not automatically private or cheap. On-chain transparency and gas costs are trade-offs developers must manage.

screens.title: Gas Efficiency and Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Designing for gas efficiency is an essential practical skill. Some operations are inherently more expensive: storage writes cost more than computation, loops over large arrays can be costly, and deploying large contracts increases upfront gas. A common beginner mistake is to place large amounts of mutable data on-chain or to write contracts that perform unbounded loops during calls. For example, iterating through an ever-growing list on every call will consume increasing gas and eventually become unusable. Practical strategies include minimizing on-chain state, using events for historical logs rather than large arrays, and preferring mapped references instead of full array scans. Another strategy is to use lightweight initialization and modular contracts or proxy patterns to reduce deployment costs. Remember also that gas price fluctuations mean that an operation that was cheap yesterday may be costly today. A helpful habit is to profile gas usage during testing and expose reasonable fee estimates to users in the UI. As a takeaway, plan for gas early in design: identify high-cost operations, refactor to cheaper patterns, and test under realistic scenarios to protect your users from unexpectedly high fees.

keyIdea.title: Gas-aware design
keyIdea.text: Avoid storing large mutable state, unbounded loops, and expensive writes; profile gas during development and design cheaper patterns.

content.html:
Best Practices › Gas Efficiency
Reduce cost by design
Identify expensive patterns and use cheaper alternatives where possible.
Expensive patterns
Storing large arrays, unbounded loops, and heavy initialization increase gas dramatically.
Cheaper alternatives
Use mappings, emit events for history, split work across multiple transactions, and profile gas usage.
Key Takeaway

Plan for gas at the architecture stage and profile functions to prevent expensive surprises for users.

Concrete example
Replace full-array scans with indexed mappings and pagination to avoid O(n) costs in frequent calls.
Common mistake
Assuming off-peak costs eliminate bad patterns — poor design remains costly at any gas price.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Wrap up by committing three core concepts to memory. First, smart contracts are self-executing programs stored on-chain; they enforce coded rules and enable decentralized applications. Second, the Ethereum Virtual Machine is the replicated deterministic runtime that executes bytecode on every node; this is what guarantees consensus on contract behavior. Third, gas is the unit that measures computation and prevents abuse; you always pay gas in Ether and transaction fees equal gas used times the gas price. A common beginner trap is to treat Ether only as a currency: remember it is also the fuel for computation. Another trap is assuming on-chain equals private or free; most operations are public and cost gas. Keep these three ideas in mind as you move from reading to building: design minimal, test thoroughly, and always account for gas in your architecture choices.

keyIdea.title: Memory anchors
keyIdea.text: Smart contracts, the EVM, and gas are the foundational trio that enable programmable, decentralized applications.

content.html:
Summary › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Three short cards that capture the chapter's essentials.
Smart Contract
A self-executing program stored on-chain that enforces coded rules without intermediaries.
Ethereum Virtual Machine
The replicated, deterministic runtime that executes contract bytecode on every node.
Gas
A unit of computational effort. Total fee = Gas Used × Gas Price, paid in Ether.
Summary takeaway
Use these three anchors when designing and evaluating dApps: what runs on-chain, how it executes, and how much it costs.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these crisp reminders as you build. First: Ether is both a currency and the fuel for computation — you cannot run contracts without it. Second: Contracts are immutable on-chain programs — treat deployment as a deliberate, audited event. Third: Gas aligns incentives and prevents abuse — every operation has a cost and that cost matters for user experience and design. Before you ship, ask these questions: have I minimized unnecessary on-chain work, do I understand the gas profile of key functions, and have I protected private keys and audited contract logic? These quick checks will help you avoid common pitfalls and design resilient dApps. What to Remember means ether = fuel, contracts = immutable code, gas = cost and limit — design with these constraints in mind.. In practical terms, compact phrases to keep at hand. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Final › Quick Reminders
Quick reminders
Three short prompts to use during design and review.
Ether is fuel
You pay gas in Ether; no Ether means no on-chain operations.
Contracts are immutable
Plan upgrades carefully and audit before deployment.
Gas shapes choices
Optimize for gas to protect users and keep dApps usable under load.
A short checklist: minimize on-chain state, profile gas, audit contracts, and protect private keys before release.

fullNarratorScript:
In this short course we will follow a single idea: Ethereum took blockchain beyond money. You will learn how smart contracts let code run as enforceable agreements, how the Ethereum Virtual Machine gives every node the same execution environment, what differentiates externally owned accounts from contract accounts, and why gas is central to safe, predictable execution. We will use concrete examples, like a freelance payout automated by a contract and examining real transactions on a block explorer to ground each concept. Understanding this foundation matters because it changes how you design software: no central server enforces outcomes, the network does. A common misconception is to treat Ether as only a currency — instead think of it as fuel that permits computation. By the end of these slides you will be able to explain why Ethereum’s design choices enable decentralized applications, identify when Ethereum is a better fit than a simple-value ledger, and read a transaction fee calculation. As you start, notice the three topics listed below: comparison to Bitcoin, the smart contract model, and practical mechanics like EVM and gas. Which of those seems most important to your project right now?

Over the next slides you will build a clear mental model of how Ethereum differs from earlier blockchains and the mechanics that make it programmable. First, you will learn to distinguish Ethereum from Bitcoin by comparing their goals and scripting capabilities, which matters when choosing a platform. Second, you will form a working definition of a smart contract: a self-executing program stored on the blockchain, and you will see concrete examples such as automated payouts or scheduled distributions. Third, you will understand the EVM as the deterministic runtime that every node executes, and why determinism and a stack-based architecture are essential for consensus. Fourth, you will learn to identify the two account types—externally owned accounts controlled by private keys and contract accounts controlled by code—and why that distinction affects security and interactions. Each objective includes a small milestone to verify understanding so you can practice reading a transaction, spotting a contract address, or explaining a fee calculation. By the end of these objectives you will know not just what each component is, but why it matters in design choices and cost trade-offs when building dApps.

This second objectives page focuses on applied skills you should be able to do after studying the chapter. First, you will learn to read Gas, Gas Price, and transaction fee calculations so you can estimate costs and make deployment choices. A concrete practice is to compute a transaction fee using the Gas Used times the Gas Price and to reason about why fees spike during congestion. Second, you will use a block explorer to inspect blocks and transactions, noticing fields such as block height, timestamp, parent hash, and gas used; seeing real data reinforces the concepts. Third, you will inspect a verified smart contract in a block explorer to read its public functions and to practice identifying whether an address is an EOA or a contract account. Fourth, you will adopt one habit for gas efficiency: examine contract operations and prefer cheaper patterns when possible. Each card includes a verified competency milestone so you can self-check progress and form better design habits when building dApps.

Start by anchoring the difference in purpose. Bitcoin's core innovation was a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that focuses on secure value transfer and intentionally limited scripting to reduce risk and complexity. Ethereum was designed from the outset to be a platform for arbitrary computation and programmable agreements — a world computer that can run smart contracts. That difference is not academic: a limited scripting language reduces the attack surface and keeps the protocol simple, while a Turing-complete environment increases flexibility but also opens new categories of risk and cost. A concrete example: Bitcoin scripts can validate simple spending conditions like multi-signature or time-locks. Ethereum smart contracts can implement a full escrow workflow that holds funds, checks off conditions, and releases payment automatically. A common misconception is that one is strictly "better" than the other; instead they are designed for different trade-offs. When deciding which chain to use, ask whether you need arbitrary business logic on-chain. If so, Ethereum’s model and the EVM are purpose-built for that work. As a takeaway, think about your application requirements: if you need programmability and on-chain enforcement, Ethereum is the better fit; if you only need a secure, minimal settlement layer, Bitcoin’s constraints may be desirable.

A smart contract is a program stored on the blockchain that runs exactly as programmed when triggered by transactions. Think of it as a self-executing agreement: the terms are written in code and enforced by the network instead of a court or a central server. A concrete example is a freelancer payment contract that releases funds once the job status is set to complete. Because the code and state are stored on-chain, results are immutable and censorship-resistant. That immutability is powerful but comes with caveats: bugs cannot be patched without careful upgrade patterns, and every operation costs gas to execute. One common misconception is to equate a smart contract with a legal contract; they are not the same. Smart contracts enforce coded logic, but they may not address off-chain disputes or real-world verification unless the contract is paired with oracles or other verification mechanisms. In practice, designers must decide which parts of a workflow belong on-chain and which remain off-chain to balance transparency, cost, and upgradability. As a takeaway, define a small on-chain core of trustless logic and keep heavy or mutable processes off-chain. How would you split responsibility for a payments workflow between on-chain code and an off-chain verifier?

The Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM, is the runtime environment that executes smart contract bytecode on every participating node. Conceptually, you can think of the EVM as a global, decentralized computer: when a transaction calls a contract function, the contract’s bytecode is executed by the EVM to produce a new state. Because the same bytecode runs on every node, determinism is essential — all nodes must agree on the result to reach consensus. The EVM is stack-based: operations push and pop values to a stack, which is simpler to reason about for bytecode interpretation. It is also Turing-complete, meaning it can represent any computation given enough resources. However, the EVM limits resource consumption through gas so that long-running or infinite computations are impossible without payment. A concrete example is a token transfer function: its bytecode updates balances and emits an event; every node runs those same steps and updates local state identically. A common misconception is to imagine the EVM as a single machine; in reality, it is a replicated execution environment running independently on many machines to ensure the same result. As a takeaway, design contracts to be deterministic and gas-aware so the EVM can run them efficiently and securely.

Ethereum distinguishes two account types that are central to how users and contracts interact. Externally Owned Accounts, or EOAs, are controlled by private keys held by people or services; they can sign transactions, send Ether, and call contracts. Contract Accounts are controlled by code: they are created when a contract is deployed and have no private key. They can hold Ether and tokens, and they execute their code when called by an EOA or another contract. A concrete example: using a wallet like MetaMask manages an EOA — you sign a transaction that calls a contract method to swap tokens. The contract account then runs its code and updates storage and balances. A common misconception is to assume that contract accounts 'belong' to a person — in reality they act by their code and any privileges are encoded into that code. Security implications flow from this distinction: EOAs custody private keys and are susceptible to private key compromise, while contract accounts are susceptible to logic bugs. As a takeaway, when designing a dApp, explicitly decide which operations require human signatures and which should be delegated to contract logic, and plan key management and upgradeability strategies accordingly.

Gas is a measure of computational effort on Ethereum. Every basic operation in a transaction or contract execution consumes a specific amount of gas. When you submit a transaction you specify a gas limit and a gas price; validators execute instructions and charge for the gas used. The essential purpose of gas is twofold: it prevents malicious or accidental infinite loops and runaway computation by making each operation cost something, and it fairly compensates validators for processing transactions. A concrete analogy in the chapter is fuel for a car: Ether is the currency used to pay for gas, which is the resource measured during computation. A common beginner mistake is to think of gas as a separate currency — it is actually a unit, and you pay for it in Ether; the fee equals gas used times gas price. Another practical point is that gas prices change with network demand, so complex operations are more expensive during congestion. As a takeaway, always estimate gas for your smart contract functions and design gas-efficient logic so users do not face unexpectedly high costs.

A practical formula you will use repeatedly is simple: total transaction fee equals Gas Used times Gas Price. Gas Used is the actual number of gas units consumed while executing your transaction or contract call. Gas Price is how much Ether you are willing to pay per gas unit. Combined they yield the fee paid in Ether. For example, if a transaction uses 50,000 gas and the gas price is 20 gwei, multiply those to get the transaction cost (in this case convert gwei to Ether to get the final amount). Why does this matter? Because both factors affect cost and latency: higher gas price encourages validators to include your transaction sooner, and more complex contract operations increase gas used. A common misconception is to ignore Gas Used when estimating cost — optimizations that reduce gas used directly reduce user expense. Another important detail from the chapter is that network demand makes gas prices vary, so the same operation can cost more or less depending on congestion. As a takeaway, always test and estimate gas consumption for common functions and communicate likely costs to users so they can make informed decisions about interacting with your dApp.

When you deploy a smart contract, the compiler produces bytecode that is stored on-chain as the contract account’s code. That bytecode is what the EVM executes when the contract is called. Deployment is itself a transaction: it stores the bytecode in a new contract account and consumes gas proportional to code size and constructor work. When a user later calls a function, the transaction provides input data and the EVM steps through the bytecode deterministically, updating storage and producing any events or returns. A concrete example: a simple token contract compiles to bytecode that implements balance updates, transfer checks, and emits events. A common misconception is to think source code is required at runtime — the EVM only runs bytecode; source code may be verified and published for human readability, but the network executes compiled code. As a developer, remember that deployment costs can be large because storing code on-chain consumes gas; that is why minimizing unnecessary code and using libraries or proxy patterns can be important. Consider deployment as an investment: once code is stored immutably, its behavior governs future interactions unless upgrade patterns are used.
